common_name: Kingston Black Apple (Classic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Kingston Black is notoriously shy-bearing and susceptible to scab, so site it in an open spot with good air circulation.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Kingston Black is notoriously shy-bearing and susceptible to scab, so site it in an open spot with good air circulation. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, dark red-purple apple is the most celebrated of the true single-variety, or vintage, cider apples, prized as a rare bittersharp carrying both the tannin and acid balance needed to produce a complex, well-structured cider entirely on its own without blending. Its fruit is far too astringent and acidic for fresh eating, but its combination of tannin, sugar, and acid in a single apple has made it the benchmark variety against which other cider apples are measured. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and expect a light, sometimes biennial crop, since Kingston Black is well known among cider makers for being a difficult, temperamental tree to grow well.

Originating in Somerset, England, this small, red-flushed apple is one of the most widely planted bittersweet cider apples in both traditional English cider and the modern American craft cider industry, valued for contributing soft, rounded tannin and moderate sugar that blends smoothly with sharper or more acidic varieties. Unlike the temperamental Kingston Black, it is a reliable, consistent, heavy-bearing tree that ripens late in the season and tolerates a range of growing conditions reasonably well, making it a popular starting point for home cider orchardists. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the small, tannic fruit is grown exclusively for cider rather than fresh eating.

Named for a mill in Somerset, England, near which the original seedling tree was found, this attractive pink-blushed apple is a classic bittersweet cider variety producing soft, mellow tannin and good juice volume, widely planted both in traditional West Country English cider orchards and in newer American craft cider plantings. Its early, showy pink spring bloom makes it ornamentally attractive as well as productive, and it is a consistent, moderately vigorous bearer that combines well with sharper or bittersharp varieties in a cider blend. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Somerset Redstreak Apple (Historic Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Somerset Redstreak is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from a wide planting spacing.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Somerset Redstreak is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from a wide planting spacing. A traditional West Country English cider apple distinct from the unrelated old Redstreak variety once famous in Herefordshire, it produces a reliable crop of medium, red-streaked bittersweet fruit valued by cider makers for good, well-balanced tannin and juice yield in a full-flavored traditional English-style cider blend. Its vigorous, spreading growth habit and reliable annual bearing have kept it in cultivation in traditional Somerset cider orchards for generations, even as many other historic regional varieties have become rare. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Harry Masters Jersey Apple (Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Harry Masters Jersey is a reliable, productive variety well suited to traditional cider blends.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Harry Masters Jersey is a reliable, productive variety well suited to traditional cider blends. A West Country English cider apple prized for producing consistently high-tannin, well-structured bittersweet juice, it is one of the workhorse varieties of traditional Somerset and Devon cider blends, valued more for the reliable quality of its juice than for the tree's ornamental qualities. Its medium-sized, dull red-flushed fruit is grown exclusively for milling and pressing, and it pairs well in a blend with sharper, more acidic apples to round out the finished cider's structure. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is far too astringent for fresh eating.

common_name: Foxwhelp Apple (Historic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Foxwhelp is an old, variable seedling-origin variety, so named-clone stock is preferable to seed-grown trees for predictable fruit quality.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Foxwhelp is an old, variable seedling-origin variety, so named-clone stock is preferable to seed-grown trees for predictable fruit quality. One of the oldest documented English cider apples, traced back to seventeenth-century Herefordshire, it is a classic bittersharp valued for high acidity balanced with substantial tannin, producing a sharp, vigorous, long-keeping cider prized by traditional cider makers for its aging potential. Its long history has led to several slightly different clonal strains circulating under the same name, so sourcing named, virus-indexed nursery stock rather than seedlings gives the most reliable fruit quality. Harvest in early-to-mid fall, notably earlier than many other classic cider apples, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Brown Snout Apple (Herefordshire Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Brown Snout is a late-ripening, reliably productive variety valued in traditional Herefordshire cider blends.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Brown Snout is a late-ripening, reliably productive variety valued in traditional Herefordshire cider blends. A traditional Herefordshire, England cider apple named for the distinctive russeted, elongated end of its small, dull orange-brown fruit, it is a well-regarded bittersweet variety contributing good tannin structure and moderate sugar to a blended cider, and it remains a component of some well-known commercial English cider blends. It ripens late in the season, later than many other classic cider varieties, and stores reasonably well after harvest before milling, giving cider makers some flexibility in scheduling the press. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press once fully ripe, since the astringent fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.
